articles.title: Meet Jawad Khalfan, the Long Island entrepreneur who started a security company from a garage in 2020; six years later, SecureTech Systems has completed more than 1,500 installations and won a 2026 state entrepreneurship award
articles.summary: A small security business launched in 2020 has grown into a Long Island technology company with more than 1,500 installations to its name.
articles.body: A small security business launched in 2020 has grown into a Long Island technology company with more than 1,500 installations to its name. SecureTech Systems, co-founded by Jawad Khalfan, was recently recognised as the 2026 Next-Gen Entrepreneur of the Year by the New York Small Business Development Centers (New York SBDC). The award was announced as part of the organisation’s statewide client awards programme, which selected recipients from more than 27,000 small-business clients. The New York SBDC, SecureTech Systems and industry publication SDM Magazine provide details about the company’s growth, services and evolution from residential work towards larger commercial projects.Khalfan launched SecureTech Systems in April 2020 with business partner Joseph Kessler. In a 2025 account of the company’s fifth anniversary, Khalfan described the early years as a period of uncertainty and persistence, with the business having initially operated from a much smaller setup before developing into an established company. The Better Business Bureau lists SecureTech Systems as having been incorporated on April 9, 2020, with Khalfan as CEO and co-founder.Today, SecureTech operates from Garden City South, New York, and works as a low-voltage technology integrator rather than simply an alarm installer. Its services cover areas including video surveillance, access control, networking, audio-visual systems and other integrated security technologies. The company says its work spans commercial buildings, schools, healthcare facilities, managed properties and other institutional environments.One of the biggest changes in the company’s trajectory has been its move towards commercial security. The New York SBDC’s account of the award notes that SecureTech initially had a heavier focus on residential projects before Khalfan shifted the company’s attention towards commercial installations and larger opportunities. That change has helped shape the type of work the company takes on today. (LinkedIn⁠ )The shift can be seen in SecureTech’s work with educational institutions. A case study published by security technology manufacturer AtlasIED details a Long Island school project involving surveillance cameras, card access control, networking upgrades, low-voltage cabling and a mass-notification system. More than 80 classrooms received new communication equipment as part of the upgrade, illustrating the broader range of technology involved in modern security projects.The company has also accumulated recognition before its latest state award. Khalfan was named to Long Island Business News’ 30 Under 30 list in 2023, while SecureTech Systems has also been recognised in connection with business and entrepreneurship programmes. Its own awards record lists a 2023 Rising Star Under 30 recognition, a 2024 Rookie of the Year finalist position and a 2024 Diversity in Business award for Khalfan.The 2026 New York SBDC award adds another milestone to that progression. SecureTech Systems was scheduled for its Next-Gen Entrepreneur of the Year celebration on September 16, with the Long Island SBDC at Stony Brook University supporting the business and Robert B. Harrison serving as its business adviser. The recognition comes six years after the company was established and follows its expansion from a small startup into a business reporting more than 1,500 completed installations.For Khalfan, the story of SecureTech Systems is ultimately tied to a change in scale as much as a change in technology: a business that began during a difficult economic period has gradually moved towards larger commercial projects, more sophisticated security systems and a broader role as a technology partner for organisations across Long Island and the wider New York area.You use AI every day. articles.title: PM Modi recalls 2016 surgical strikes on Mann Ki Baat, says terrorism will get decisive response
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday recalled the 2016 surgical strikes carried out by the Indian Army across the Line of Control (LoC),
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday recalled the 2016 surgical strikes carried out by the Indian Army across the Line of Control (LoC), saying India has made it clear that terrorism will be met with a “strong and decisive response”.Addressing the 138th episode of his monthly radio programme Mann Ki Baat, PM Modi said the surgical strikes, carried out on September 28-29, 2016, demonstrated India's resolve to respond to cross-border terrorism.“A major historical achievement of India is set to complete 10 years in just a day—the surgical strike. Ten years ago, on September 28–29, 2016, the Indian Army conducted a surgical strike on terrorist hideouts in PoJK. The world was astonished by the manner in which our brave soldiers crossed the Line of Control (LoC) to take action against terrorism,” he said.PM Modi said the operation had demonstrated a new approach to India's counter-terrorism policy.“The surgical strike boldly demonstrated a new example of India's counter-terrorism policy to the entire world. It served as our decisive response to the long-standing suffering India had endured due to terrorist attacks,” he said.“India has made it clear that terrorism will be met with a strong and decisive response,” PM Modi added.The Prime Minister also referred to the Balakot airstrike and Operation Sindoor, saying India had repeatedly sent the same message in response to terrorism.“Over the past decade, from the Balakot airstrike to 'Operation Sindoor', India has repeatedly sent a clear message: if terrorists dare to cast a hostile eye on India, they will face a befitting response,” he said.PM Modi also asserted that India was following a policy of “zero tolerance against terrorism”.The surgical strikes were carried out in response to the 2016 Uri terror attack, with the Indian Army targeting terror launch pads across the LoC.Other highlights from Mann Ki BaatThe Prime Minister also referred to the ongoing Census exercise, describing it as a “national responsibility” and saying every citizen had a role to play. He said the first phase of the Census was almost complete across all states and Union territories, with information on more than 32 crore families already recorded. He urged people to actively participate in the exercise and make use of the online enumeration facility.With October 2 approaching, PM Modi also highlighted cleanliness initiatives being carried out by communities across the country and recalled Mahatma Gandhi's emphasis on cleanliness.“October 2nd is just a few days away; it is the birth anniversary of Revered Bapu. Bapu gave us many mantras for life; cleanliness is one of them,” he said.PM Modi cited examples of youngsters cleaning a river in Madhya Pradesh, restoring old stepwells and wells in Andhra Pradesh, volunteers cleaning Mumbai beaches and young people in Delhi spreading awareness about waste segregation. He also mentioned students and local residents in West Bengal who were cleaning picnic spots.“One thing is clearly evident in all these efforts: it started with one person, then others joined in and the caravan grew. This is public participation,” PM Modi said.“Cleanliness is also the most beautiful tribute we can pay to Bapu,” he added.PM Modi also spoke about the fight against narcotics and said young people were coming together to spread awareness against drug addiction through the Nasha Mukt Yuva Abhiyan. He said millions of young people had taken a pledge to stay away from drugs and had also taken responsibility for spreading the message among others.The Prime Minister also recalled the history of the Somnath temple, saying those who sought to erase India's identity by destroying it ultimately had no existence. He said the temple continued to stand in its grandeur by the sea, blessing India with immortality.During the broadcast, PM Modi also paid tribute to late VHP leader Ashok Singhal on his birth anniversary, recalling his contribution to the Ram Janmabhoomi movement and describing his life as that of an ascetic who remained engaged with society.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: Ed Sheeran’s two sold-out concerts at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, were canceled just hours before the scheduled performances as a
articles.body: Ed Sheeran’s two sold-out concerts at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, were canceled just hours before the scheduled performances as a powerful nor’easter threatened New England. The cancellation was reported by the BBC, CBS Boston and Boston 25 News, with the venue and tour promoter pointing to severe weather conditions and safety concerns. The shows, scheduled for Friday, September 25, and Saturday, September 26, were part of Sheeran’s ongoing Loop Tour. Both dates were listed as canceled on Ticketmaster, with the concerts originally scheduled to begin at 8 p.m.The decision came as a major fall nor’easter moved toward the region, bringing the threat of heavy rain, strong winds, coastal flooding and rough surf across parts of New England. The Massachusetts shows were therefore already among the most closely watched dates on the Loop Tour. articles.title: Meet Ruoqi Li, 16, and Jason Yang, 17, the California teens who built an AI fall-risk system for older adults using a smartphone and wearable sensors; their project won a shared $100,000 Davidson scholarship
articles.summary: Two California teenagers, Ruoqi Li, 16, and Jason Yang, 17, have developed an artificial intelligence-powered system designed to identify fall risks in
articles.body: Two California teenagers, Ruoqi Li, 16, and Jason Yang, 17, have developed an artificial intelligence-powered system designed to identify fall risks in older adults before a fall occurs. According to Davidson Institute, the project, called SafeStrides, combines a smartphone application with wearable sensors to analyse walking patterns and provide an assessment of a person's fall risk.Li, a junior at The Harker School in San Jose, and Yang, a senior at Head-Royce School, developed the project as a way to make fall-risk assessment more accessible outside medical facilities. Their work has now earned them recognition as 2026 Davidson Fellows and a shared $100,000 scholarship in the engineering category.The teenagers said their interest in the problem was influenced by seeing family members suffer serious injuries after falls. As they researched the issue, they found that falls are a major cause of injury and injury-related death among older adults. The project description by the Davidson Institute says one in four older adults falls every year.With SafeStrides, instead of waiting for a fall to happen or relying only on occasional assessments at a clinic, an older adult could use a smartphone and wearable sensors at home for regular screening. The system collects movement data and uses AI to identify changes that could indicate an increased risk of falling.How SafeStrides worksSafeStrides uses a smartphone camera and wearable sensors to study how an older person walks. During a short guided test, the application collects video and sensor data and combines them for an assessment.The wearable system uses inertial measurement units, or IMUs, along with pressure insoles. An IMU can capture movement-related information, while pressure insoles provide data about how a person places weight on their feet. These different types of information are brought together so the system can examine walking and movement in more detail.The smartphone application synchronises the sensor data with a live camera feed. It then uses multimodal AI to produce an evaluation of fall risk. The system also gives practical suggestions related to mobility and home safety.SafeStrides is intended to identify changes months before a fall happens, allowing older adults to take steps towards improving mobility and safety.The system was developed to address limitations the teenagers identified in conventional fall-risk assessments. According to their project description, clinical assessments can require older adults to travel to medical facilities and can depend on physician availability. They also said many people are screened only once a year, which may make it harder to identify rapid changes in physical condition.From a bulky prototype to wearable sensorsBuilding the system also required several rounds of engineering work. The first version of SafeStrides was an Arduino-based prototype. Although it worked, the teenagers said it was bulky and could only process the collected information after testing was completed.They then developed a second-generation system using IMUs, pressure insoles, an ESP32 microcontroller and Bluetooth modules. These changes allowed them to create a system that could collect and transmit sensor information in real time.A third generation focused on the physical design of the wearable system. The teenagers made it more compact and lightweight so it could be worn more comfortably and without getting in the way of normal movement.At the same time, they developed a cross-platform mobile application using Flutter. The app connects to the wearable hardware through Bluetooth and automatically synchronises high-frequency sensor streams with live camera footage.This created a single system in which movement captured by the wearable sensors and the smartphone camera can be analysed together. The teenagers describe this combination as a multimodal approach because it brings together different forms of data instead of relying on just one measurement.Designed for use at home and in clinicsSafeStrides is intended to work both at home and in clinical settings. At home, the system could allow older adults to complete guided assessments without travelling to a medical facility. The app can then provide an immediate evaluation and suggestions related to mobility and home safety.Meanwhile, medical assistants could use SafeStrides to conduct fall-risk evaluations without requiring direct physician involvement for every screening. The teenagers said this could make assessments more consistent and easier to carry out.Their project description says the system is designed for the world's 1.2 billion older adults. They also said it could help shift fall prevention away from occasional screening towards more continuous monitoring.The approach is different from reactive medical alert devices, which are generally intended to notify someone after a fall has already happened.For Li, the Davidson Fellowship is also connected to her plans for the future. She said she wants to study an interdisciplinary subject combining artificial intelligence and healthcare and hopes to develop technologies that improve quality of life."To me, being recognized as a Davidson Fellow not only represents personal achievement but also inspires me to turn technical research into practical tools that help others, proving that young innovators can tackle society’s most urgent challenges. I am honored and excited to join the community of Davidson Fellows," Li said.Yang plans to study electrical or systems engineering and continue working on embedded technologies. He has previously built circuits, developed real-time data processing systems and designed mechanical components for functional prototypes."I’m incredibly honored to be a Davidson Fellow. This recognition affirms our commitment to developing practical, human-centered technologies and raising awareness of early fall risk detection in older adults," Yang said."By making fall risk assessment more accessible and proactive, we hope to encourage earlier intervention and help more seniors maintain their safety, health and independence," he added.The Davidson Institute listed Li and Yang among the 2026 Davidson Fellows receiving a $100,000 scholarship in engineering. The fellowship recognises students aged 18 and younger for significant achievements and innovative projects.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Vijay government exempts Tamil Nadu Public (Law & Order) department from RTI- what it means
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Tamil Nadu government led by CM C Joseph Vijay has exempted the Public (Law and Order) Department from the ambit of the Right to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Tamil Nadu government led by CM C Joseph Vijay has exempted the Public (Law and Order) Department from the ambit of the Right to Information (RTI) Act, classifying it as an Intelligence and Security Organisation under Section 24(4) of the law.A Gazette notification issued by the state government places the department under the exemption framework applicable to intelligence and security organisations. The move means information held by the department will generally be outside the scope of RTI requests, subject to the statutory exceptions under the Act.What the exemption meansThe Public (Law and Order) Department deals with matters concerning policing, public order and law-and-order administration and RTI Act is a law to provide for setting out the practical regime of right to information for citizens wherein they can secure access to information under the control of public authorities.This exemption could therefore affect RTI requests seeking information relating to communal incidents, political agitations, police actions and other law-and-order matters handled by the department.The statement reads, "Gazette notification dated September 21, 2026, issued by the Human Resources Management Department, the Governor, exercising powers under Section 24(4) of the Right to Information Act, 2005, has specified the Public (Law and Order) Department as an "Intelligence and Security Organization" established by the Tamil Nadu government, "for which the said Act shall not apply."However, Section 24 of the RTI Act does not provide a blanket exemption. Even organisations covered by the provision are required to provide information relating to allegations of corruption and human-rights violations, subject to the procedure prescribed under the law.Tamil Nadu has previously used the provision to exclude organisations including the Tamil Nadu State Vigilance Commission and the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1998, an Ontario fourth-grader dropped a note into Lake St. Clair; 26 years later, it turned up in her daughter’s fourth-grade class at the same school
articles.summary: In an extraordinary twist of fate, a note dropped into Lake St. Clair by a fourth-grade student in 1998 was found by her daughter in 2024 at the same school, creating a beautiful bond across generations.
articles.body: In 1998, a fourth grader named Makenzie Morris typed out a letter about the waters of the Great Lakes on a computer in her classroom, as part of a class assignment from her teacher, Roland St. Pierre, at St. John the Baptist Catholic Elementary School in Belle River, Ontario. Once the letter was printed, nine-year-old Makenzie rolled it up, sealed it inside a plastic bottle with wax, and walked with her classmates to a pier where the Belle River empties into Lake St. Clair. There, roughly 32 students let their bottles go into the water, most likely never expecting to hear from them again. Twenty-six years later, in the fall of 2024, one of those bottles surfaced near the pier on the same lake where it had been thrown in. It was found by a kindergartner from the very same school, and it eventually made its way into a fourth-grade classroom where Makenzie's own daughter, now a student there herself, happened to be sitting.How the bottle resurfaced after nearly three decadesRiver Vandenberg, a St. John the Baptist student, found the bottle along the sandbar of Belle River pier in Lake St. Clair when he went exploring with his grandmother, Michele. As per Good Morning America, the rolled-up letter within was written by Makenzie Morris, now known by her married name Van Eyk, a nine-year-old student of Roland St. Pierre's fourth-grade class at the time. In fact, the letter contained instructions for whoever would find it to contact the school. Michele thought the letter could be part of some school activity and contacted the school directly without considering that it may be just trash. Her guess proved right very quickly. The teacher at the school responded immediately and informed them that the letter dated back to 1998, 26 years earlier. As per CBC News, St. Pierre, who is now retired, recalled that he had assigned the "message in a bottle" project to his class in 1998, and that only two other bottles from that group have since turned up: one appeared weeks later in Tecumseh, which is located 10 miles away from Belle River, while the other one appeared a year after that in Lake Erie, an outlier that the local wind-driven currents described below don't fully explain.Why a bottle could stay near the same shoreline for 26 yearsLake St. Clair's own physical characteristics help explain why a sealed bottle might resurface so close to where it was originally thrown in rather than drifting far away. A technical report from NOAA's Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory, Lake St. Clair Physical and Hydraulic Characteristics, discusses how the lake is described as having a shallow bottom whose surface currents are determined mainly by wind direction, not by strong currents. Since the lake lies between the inflowing St. Clair River and the outflowing Detroit River, it would make sense for the water movements to be influenced by winds and not just flow in one direction towards the river, thus giving anything floating a chance to get back into place instead of being washed away completely.A separate field study from the US Geological Survey adds more direct evidence of this behavior. In Visualization of a Drifting Buoy Deployment on Lake St. Clair, researchers deployed twelve drifting buoys in the lake for 74 hours in August 2002 to analyze the circulation patterns of the lake as part of a water intake safety evaluation project. It was determined by the aforementioned researchers that the movement of the buoys depended largely on the prevailing winds at the time, such that the buoys would not always move in a direct line towards the outflow point but sometimes even in loops and sometimes backwards instead. Such erratic movement due to the wind is characteristic of a closed bottle that stays within the same general vicinity of shore for many years.Why the letter landed in her daughter's classroomRiver took the bottle to school, where a teacher from the fourth-grade class read the letter to the other children, an event which would turn out to involve Makenzie's own daughter, Scarlet Van Eyk. According to Smithsonian Magazine, Scarlet was present when the letter was read and recognized her mother's maiden name in it right away. Scarlet told CBC News that her jaw just dropped, and that as soon as classmates began asking her who had written the letter, she had to tell them that her own mother had written it. But that wasn't all. Scarlet is now a fourth-grader at St. John the Baptist, in the same class as her mother was in when she wrote the letter, so both mother and daughter reached this same milestone in the same grade, at the same school. St. Pierre also pointed out another coincidence, stating that he used to teach River's father, thereby linking this family to the small school community.What the reunion meant for the family that wrote itVan Eyk mentioned that she never gave much thought to the bottle during the last twenty-six years, although she did sometimes wonder about its fate after she had thrown it into the water when she herself was just a child. Van Eyk explained that her first reaction when she received a call from the school was one of concern rather than of excitement, thinking that there could be some problem with her own child before finding out the real reason for the phone call. She then went on to say that she found the whole event unforgettable, especially since it was a child attending the same school that found the bottle.For an area such as Belle River, which is part of the Municipality of Lakeshore and is inhabited by about ten thousand people, calculating the probability of finding the closed bottle in the same vicinity where it was dumped, with the possibility that it would then pass to the same school’s student, is quite hard to estimate. St. Pierre, commenting on the results of the situation, noted that the bottle might simply go unnoticed indefinitely or be found by a person who had no relation to the school whatsoever. However, a letter written by one nine-year-old girl in 1998 was eventually read in front of a class that also included her nine-year-old daughter in 2024.You use AI every day. articles.summary: LUCKNOW: When the NEET PG 2026 results were declared on Sept 24, congratulations poured in for Sqn Ldr Pallakshi Prasad, a 28 year old medical officer
articles.body: LUCKNOW: When the NEET PG 2026 results were declared on Sept 24, congratulations poured in for Sqn Ldr Pallakshi Prasad, a 28 year old medical officer posted at Air Force Station Kanpur, after she secured All India Rank 2. Director General Armed Forces Medical Services (DGAFMS) Air Marshal Sandeep Thareja congratulated the AFMC alumni of the C3 Batch, calling it a proud achievement for the Armed Forces Medical Services.For Pallakshi, whose name means soft, the journey has been anything but easy. It has been defined by years of disciplined study, military service and an unwavering commitment to learning."I always knew I wanted to become a doctor," Pallakshi said. "Even though both my parents are engineers, they never said no to my dream. They simply supported me."Born in Ranchi and raised in Hyderabad, Pallakshi studied at Delhi Public School before cracking NEET UG 2016 with an All India Rank of 1,312, without taking a drop year. Admission rules in her home state narrowed her options, but an application to the Armed Forces Medical College (AFMC), encouraged by her mother, changed her life. Her mother, Shyamli Prasad, is a senior software engineer with Infosys.She entered AFMC after securing Girls Merit Rank 3 in the selection process and graduated sixth in overall merit in her batch. "I fell in love with the AFMC campus and everything it stood for. By the time I graduated, I didn't feel like an outsider to the uniform anymore. Taking permanent commission was a natural decision," she recalled.Commissioned into the Indian Navy on May 15, 2021, she spent nearly two and a half years as a medical officer aboard a warship before moving to the Indian Air Force in 2025. Ship service, she says, shaped both her personality and professional outlook.Preparing for one of India's toughest postgraduate medical entrance examinations while serving in uniform demanded extraordinary discipline."I used to study whenever time permitted. Between patients, after duty hours, through books and online platforms. It wasn't about long hours every day, but about being consistent," she said. Guided by mentor Dr Vineet Behera, a serving military doctor, she also presented a research paper on chronic kidney disease at the Bombay Medical Congress during her internship.She is now considering radiology, internal medicine and dermatology for specialisation.Her father, Chandra Kishore Prasad, Principal Chief Safety Officer (PCSO), Central Railway and co author of the book KAVACH: Cab Signalling & Automatic Train Protection System for Digital Railways, says the signs of determination appeared early."She always had commitment and focus. She was head girl at DPS Hyderabad and even secured second place in an international English Olympiad. When she told us she wanted to study medicine, I reminded her that becoming a doctor meant studying throughout life. Her answer was simple: 'I want to become a doctor.' We told her we would support her in whatever she chose," he said.Pallakshi says the overwhelming response after the result has been deeply moving."I've received so much love from my family, the AFMC community and the Armed Forces fraternity. I think whatever I am today is because of what AFMC and military life have shaped me into," she said.Pallakshi is married to a serving IAF doctor, and she has been posted in Kanpur since 2025.While her parents and younger brother, Prageeth Prasad, all pursued engineering and technology, Pallakshi became the family's outlier. She followed her childhood dream of becoming a doctor and later became the first in the family to serve in the Armed Forces.
